newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK leftwinger confident over Sino-US relations.
newsitem.headline: HK leftwinger confident over Sino-US relations.

text.p: The leader of Hong Kong's largest pro-Beijing party said on Thursday he was confident Sino-U.S. relations would not be knocked off course over the British colony's handover to China.

Tsang Yok-sing also quashed intense speculation that the Chinese Communist Party might set up in Hong Kong and said this was not in Beijing's plans for the territory, which is to be run under a "one country, two systems" formula.
The United States has backed the right of Hong Kong's pro-democracy activists to demonstrate when the territory switches from British rule on July 1.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is flying to Hong Kong for the handover ceremonies but will not attend the swearing-in of a controversial provisional legislature handpicked by Beijing.
Tsang, chairman of the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong Kong (DAB), was optimistic that relations between Washington and Beijing could still prosper.
"I am confident it will not cause a long-time standoff," he told a news conference called as the clock ticked away to handover day.
"We understand very clearly the feelings felt by many American politicians and congressmen towards the provisional legislature -- not that I think these feelings are justified."
Tsang forecast any row would blow over and "hopefully the sky will turn clear" once Hong Kong stages elections in the first year of Chinese rule.

The former headmaster, a political firebrand in the Cultural Revolution when he took to the streets to protest over British rule, very much doubted if China's Communist Party would set up in Hong Kong and contest its elections.
"I don't think this is desirable for the interests of Hong Kong and I don't think the Chinese government wants to see it happen," he said.

"If these Chinese Communist Party members come out, stand in elections and lose, of course that would be read by Hong Kong people as evidence that the Chinese Communist Party is not supported here," he added.

Tsang, whose brother and sister were imprisoned as teenagers in Hong Kong during the 1960's political unrest, praised Britain's administrative legacies to Hong Kong but said most of its 6.4 million people were glad the British were leaving.
He acknowledged at first having serious reservations about former shipping magnate Tung Chee-Hwa being appointed by Beijing as the colony's post-handover chief executive.
But he has now concluded: "I don't think anyone else in the same position could have done better."
"He is a very convincing man. He has charisma of a kind," Tsang told reporters at the Foreign Correspondents' Club.
